title: The overthinking tax: more reasoning tokens rarely buy better code, but always cost more — the reasoning dial is the hidden budget leak
summary: A wave of 2026 research is puncturing the 'more thinking = better answers' assumption that underpins how most teams configure reasoning models. The arXiv paper 'When More Thinking Hurts' shows that past a task-dependent threshold, extra reasoning tokens produce diminishing returns and can actively degrade accuracy — accuracy plateaus while cost climbs linearly with the reasoning budget. The economic asymmetry is brutal: because reasoning tokens are billed output tokens, they are the most expensive tokens in the request, and generating 8,000 of them costs roughly 16x a 500-token response. One documented pipeline ran extended thinking on trivial snippets and paid ~30x its expected bill (≈1,200 thinking tokens for a 30-token task). The non-obvious insight for engineering leaders: reasoning effort is a cost dial most teams leave pinned at maximum by default, paying premium output rates for compute that, on the majority of routine coding and tool-use tasks, changes nothing in the result. The right unit of account is cost-per-correct-outcome, and the right control is per-task-class reasoning budgets — not a blanket 'use the smartest, highest-effort setting everywhere' policy.
source: arXiv Preprint ('When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling'), with corroborating practitioner cost analyses
whyItMatters: Reasoning tokens are billed at the (expensive) output rate, so a default 'high effort everywhere' setting can multiply cost several-fold while accuracy has already plateaued — a pure loss most dashboards never attribute to the reasoning dial.

The optimal reasoning budget is task-dependent and often low; treating reasoning effort as a per-task-class configuration, not a global default, is a concrete lever that cuts spend without touching model choice or output quality.
This reframes vendor 'smarter reasoning' upsells: for routine, well-scoped coding and tool-calls, more thinking is often paying premium rates for motion, not results.
recommendedActions: Audit where extended/high-effort reasoning is enabled by default and measure accuracy-vs-cost at 2-3 reasoning budgets per task class to find the plateau point.
Route simple, deterministic, or tool-heavy tasks to low or no extended reasoning; reserve high-effort settings for genuinely hard, ambiguous problems.
Track a cost-per-correct-outcome metric (not cost-per-token) so overthinking shows up as wasted spend rather than hiding inside aggregate usage.
Set explicit max-reasoning-token caps in agent harnesses to prevent runaway 'thinking' on trivial calls.
risksAndCaveats: The core paper studies reasoning tasks broadly, not exclusively coding/agentic work, so the exact plateau thresholds may differ for software tasks; the coding-cost specifics come partly from practitioner reports.
Where the optimal budget sits is task- and model-specific; under-budgeting reasoning on genuinely hard problems can cut accuracy, so this is a tuning exercise, not a blanket 'turn thinking off.'
Some corroborating cost figures are anecdotal single cases and vendor/practitioner blogs, useful as illustrations of magnitude rather than precise averages.
